title: Review: Metallic bonding and comparing structures; Ionisation energies
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD06#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD06#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS05#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS05#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS05#N.11, BD06#N.3a, AS05#N.4a, BD06#N.15, AS05#N.7a, BD06#N.11, AS05#N.10a, BD06#N.13. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ductile
items.clue: Able to be drawn into wires, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Malleable
items.clue: Able to be hammered into shape, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Convergence limit
items.clue: Where hydrogen's lines for falls to n = 1 crowd together at high frequency.

items.label: Atomic radius
items.clue: The distance of the outer electron from the nucleus; it shrinks across a period.

questions.stem: Element X is in Period 3. Its first six ionisation energies are 1012, 1907, 2914, 4964, 6274 and 21 268 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement identifies X and explains the large sixth value?

options.text: X is sulfur: the jump is at the sixth ionisation energy, so X has six outer electrons.
X is phosphorus: the sixth electron is the first from the second shell, nearer the nucleus.
X is phosphorus: the sixth electron would come from a full shell, which is especially stable.
X is aluminium: the rise from 2914 to 4964 is where a new shell starts.

questions.explanation: Five electrons come from the third shell. The sixth comes from 2p: much closer to the nucleus, much less shielded, so held far more strongly.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalised electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the delocalised electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid. The metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of calcium?

options.text: Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻
Ca(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻
Ca⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + e⁻
Ca(s) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻

questions.explanation: One mole of electrons removed from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.

questions.stem: How does the first ionisation energy generally change across Period 3 from sodium to argon, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among more and more electrons.
It decreases, as the atoms get larger because more electrons are added along the period.
It increases, as atoms closer to a full outer shell resist losing any of their outer electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons have similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Nuclear charge +11 to +18; the electron removed is in the third shell, with similar shielding. 496 → 1521 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Four solids, P, Q, R and S, are tested. - P: melts at 801 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water. - Q: melts at 1085 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water. - R: melts at 114 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. - S: melts at 1710 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. Which pairing of substance and structure is correct?

options.text: P is metallic, because it conducts when molten.
Q is ionic, because it conducts when molten.
R is molecular, because it melts low and never conducts.
S is ionic, because its melting point is very high.

questions.stem: The first four successive ionisation energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. How many electrons does an atom of X have in its outer shell?

options.text: Four, as the large increase appears at the fourth ionisation energy
One, as the second value is already over three times larger than the first
Three, as the large increase comes after the third electron is removed
Thirteen, as X has atomic number 13

questions.explanation: 578 → 1817 → 2745 rise steadily; then the fourth is about four times the third. Three outer electrons: X is aluminium.

questions.stem: Silicon melts at 1414 °C. Phosphorus (white, P₄) melts at 44 °C. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Phosphorus has weaker metallic bonding, because its atoms are larger than silicon atoms.
Silicon is giant covalent, so covalent bonds break; phosphorus is P₄ molecules held by weak London forces.
Melting phosphorus breaks its P–P covalent bonds, which are much weaker than Si–Si bonds.
Silicon atoms have more electrons than P₄ molecules, so London forces between them are stronger.

questions.explanation: Melting silicon breaks strong Si–Si covalent bonds throughout the lattice. Melting P₄ overcomes only weak forces between molecules; the P–P bonds stay intact.
